title: Madame Bovary
significance: It narrates, through free indirect discourse alone and without authorial comment, how a provincial doctor's wife tries to live out the life she read about in novels and is ruined in the attempt. Prosecuted for obscenity immediately after its 1856 magazine serialization, it was acquitted in 1857 and published in book form the same year — an episode in which the method of narration itself became a matter of public dispute.

title: Salammbô
significance: A historical novel reconstructing the mercenaries' revolt in 3rd-century-BCE Carthage from archaeological and textual sources. By applying the methods of realism, previously used for contemporary settings, to an unfamiliar past without modification, it showed that realism was a method rather than a subject matter.

title: Sentimental Education
significance: Set in Paris during the revolutionary year of 1848, it records twenty years in the life of a young man who accomplishes nothing. It inverts the conventions of the coming-of-age novel, choosing a structure in which the protagonist ultimately learns nothing at all.

title: Three Tales
significance: A collection of three novellas and stories, set respectively in the 19th century, antiquity, and the Middle Ages. The first, which narrates a servant woman's entire life through a mere list of objects without ever explaining her feelings, is repeatedly cited as an example of restrained narration.

title: Bouvard and Pécuchet
significance: It catalogues, like an encyclopedia, how two retired copyists take up every field of learning in turn and fail at each. Published unfinished in 1881 after the author's death, it is, together with the dictionary of clichés planned as an appendix, an experiment that takes received opinion itself as its subject.

title: Childhood
significance: An autobiographical novella that follows, from a ten-year-old's point of view, the very order in which memory and sensation surface. It shows that its author debuted at twenty-four, an unknown writer who had already established his method of interior narration.

title: War and Peace
significance: Set in Russia during the Napoleonic Wars, it juxtaposes the lives of several families with essays on the philosophy of history within a single book. Through narration that grants an inner life to each of hundreds of characters while still preserving the scale of battle, it became the measure for the sweeping multigenerational novels that followed.

title: Anna Karenina
significance: While dealing with adultery and society's punishment for it, it runs a search for rural reform and faith in parallel. Serialized in a magazine from 1875 to 1877 and completed in book form in 1878, it is the point at which free indirect discourse and interior monologue became settled features of Russian prose.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
significance: A novella that records the last months of a successful judge dying of illness as a time in which social status becomes utterly useless. It is the standard example of narrating death not as an idea but as a continuous sequence of bodily sensation.

title: Resurrection
significance: A story in which a nobleman serving as a juror meets again, in court, the woman he once ruined, it directly indicts the institutions of justice, the church, and land ownership. The novel's depiction of church ritual became one of the triggers for his excommunication from the Orthodox Church in 1901.

title: Notes from Underground
significance: It is divided into a first part, in which a nameless retired official hurls his own misery at the reader, and a second part, which tells the story behind it. By presenting a human being who betrays his own rational self-interest, it became the prototype narrator of 20th-century existentialist narrative.

title: Crime and Punishment
significance: It tracks, in something close to real time, the consciousness of a poor student after he murders an elderly pawnbroker. It is a case of a crime novel's narrative drive and ideological argument operating simultaneously within a single narrative.

title: The Idiot
significance: It experiments with how a figure possessing nothing but good will is destroyed upon entering high society. It poses head-on the formal question of whether a novel can hold together with a wholly good man as its protagonist.

title: Demons
significance: A political novel reconstructing a murder inside a revolutionary organization, based on the 1869 Nechaev affair. By narrating the process through which ideology turns people into disposable material, it became a precedent for the totalitarian novel of the 20th century.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
significance: Centered on the brothers' trial over their father's murder, it carries the debate between faith and atheism, in the characters' own voices, all the way through on equal terms. This structure, in which the author renders judgment on neither side, is the primary evidence cited for the concept of polyphony.

title: Ward No. 6
significance: A novella in which the conversation between an asylum patient and his doctor is overturned until the doctor himself becomes a patient. By making the ward readable as a miniature of society as a whole, it drew a large response as soon as it was published.

title: The Seagull
significance: A four-act play in which a young writer demanding a new theatrical form and established artists talk past one another at a country estate. After its premiere failed in 1896, its 1898 revival by the Moscow Art Theatre succeeded, making it the starting point of 20th-century theater.

title: The Lady with the Dog
significance: It ends, without resolution, the process by which a light affair at a resort town becomes real life for both people involved. It is counted as the standard form of the modern short story that ends not in a plot twist but in a minute shift of perception.

title: Three Sisters
significance: A four-act play about three sisters who grow old in the provinces while doing nothing but repeat their wish to return to Moscow. It is the work in which the technique of dialogue that fails to answer itself, lines talking past one another, is realized most precisely.

title: The Cherry Orchard
significance: It deals with a declining landowning family losing its estate; Chekhov himself classified it as a comedy, but the premiere staged it as a tragedy. It is his last work, and it shows the changing of the classes not as an event but as the mere passage of time.

title: Peer Gynt
significance: A five-act verse play in which a braggart wanders the world yet fails to become himself. Treating the emptiness of the self through the form of folktale and fantasy, it touches the same problem as his later prose realist plays, but from the opposite direction.

title: A Doll's House
significance: A three-act play in which a marriage comes apart over the three days it takes for a forged signature to come to light. The ending, in which the wife leaves the house and shuts the door behind her, ended the convention by which European theater supplied moral reconciliation at the close.

title: Ghosts
significance: A three-act play in which a disease from a concealed past returns in the son. By putting hereditary illness and venereal disease on stage, it had its performances blocked in several countries, becoming a symbolic case of the clash between censorship and modern drama.

title: The Wild Duck
significance: It depicts how the idealism that insists truth must be told destroys a family. While refuting the structure of his own earlier plays of exposure, it introduced the symbol of the wild duck in the attic into the realist stage.

title: Hedda Gabler
significance: A four-act play in which a woman whose possibilities have been sealed off manipulates other people's lives and destroys herself in the process. Through a characterization that never explains her motives, it created a role that 20th-century acting technique has repeatedly returned to challenge.

title: Daisy Miller
significance: It narrates a young American woman who disregards European convention entirely through the eyes of a Europeanized American man. It is the novella in which James's two methods — the international theme and the restricted point of view — first come together.

title: The Portrait of a Lady
significance: It traces how an American woman who has inherited a fortune exercises her freedom and, as a result, chooses her own prison. The night-vigil scene, which fills an entire chapter with a single character's consciousness and no event at all, is the passage James himself named as his finest achievement in the preface to the New York Edition.

title: The Art of Fiction
significance: A polemical essay that refutes the received idea that a novel requires a moral purpose or a fixed kind of event, and defines the novel instead as a form that organizes impressions of experience. It is cited as the founding document of Anglophone novel theory.

title: The Turn of the Screw
significance: A ghost story conveyed entirely through a governess's manuscript, the text never settles whether the ghosts are real or the narrator's hallucination. It is the standard example of a structure in which the reader must judge the narrator's reliability.

title: The Ambassadors
significance: It narrates, strictly within the bounds of what a single consciousness perceives, how a middle-aged man who goes to Paris to bring a young man home comes to re-judge his own life. It is the completed form of the late style, the work James himself named as his finest.

title: Heart of Darkness
significance: A frame novel in which a sailor who once traveled up the Congo River tells of his voyage aboard an anchored ship. Serialized in a magazine in 1899 and collected in book form in 1902, it exposes, through its narrative structure itself, the gap between the language of empire and its actual violence.

title: Lord Jim
significance: It reconstructs, over and over, a single moment in which a ship's officer abandoned his vessel, through multiple testimonies and a scrambled chronology. This narration, which allows a single fact to be approached only from multiple angles, became a standard technique of the 20th-century novel.

title: Nostromo
significance: It narrates, through a scattered chronology, how a silver mine in a fictional South American country determines politics, revolution, and personal betrayal. It created the form of a political novel whose true protagonist is capital.

title: The Secret Agent
significance: A novel that narrates, with cold irony, a double agent in London and the anarchists' bomb plot. Based on the 1894 Greenwich Observatory bombing, it drew terrorism and the intelligence services into the novel as subject matter.

title: Under Western Eyes
significance: It transcribes, through the eyes of an English teacher, how a Russian student who informed on a comrade is sent to Geneva. By passing a Russian-novel subject through a Western narrator, it makes narrative distance itself the problem.

title: The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas
significance: An already-dead narrator calls out to the reader and lays out his own life across 160 short chapters. Written at the height of realism, it turned narrative order, reliability, and completeness all into objects of a joke, and changed the direction of the Brazilian novel.

title: The Alienist
significance: A novella in which a doctor commits the townspeople to an asylum one after another, then completely reverses his own diagnostic criteria. In the form of comedy, it argues that the line between sanity and madness is nothing but the authority of whoever does the classifying.

title: Quincas Borba
significance: It traces the ruin of a man who inherits a pseudo-philosophy justifying the survival of the winner. Taking a supporting character from the earlier novel as its title, it turns the way ideas circulate into narrative in itself.

title: Dom Casmurro
significance: A narrator seized by jealousy recalls his wife's betrayal, but every piece of evidence is his testimony alone. Thanks to its structure of leaving the verdict to the reader, interpretive debate over it has continued for more than a century.

title: Counselor Ayres' Memorial
significance: His last novel, in the form of a retired diplomat's diary, leaves behind nothing but the observations of old age. Having nearly eliminated event and left only the recorder's gaze, it is the destination his narrative experiments finally reached.

title: The Flowers of Evil
significance: A poetry collection that treats boredom, the city, death, and sensuality within the strict form of formal verse. Prosecuted for obscenity immediately after publication, it had six poems ordered removed by the court, and the Parisian Scenes sequence was added in the expanded 1861 edition.

title: Artificial Paradises
significance: A prose work that records the states of consciousness produced by opium and hashish and calculates their cost. Adapting and commenting on De Quincey's confessions of an opium eater, it moved artificial intoxication into a question of aesthetics.

title: The Painter of Modern Life
significance: A critical essay that, in discussing the illustrator Constantin Guys, defines modernity as the attitude of extracting the eternal from the transient. It became the grounds for art's claim that it may treat the surface of its own age as a legitimate subject.

title: Paris Spleen
significance: A posthumously published collection of 50 short poems written in prose, free of the constraints of meter. It established the prose poem as a genre in its own right, enabling 20th-century poetry to operate outside fixed form.

title: Leaves of Grass
significance: A self-published first edition of 95 pages, made up of twelve untitled poems and a prose preface. Its free verse and list form were already complete, and it was expanded and rearranged under the same title until his death.

title: Drum-Taps
significance: A collection of war poems written while he tended the wounded in Civil War field hospitals. Together with the elegies for Lincoln included in its sequel, it recast war not as a tale of heroism but as a record of the body and of caregiving.

title: Democratic Vistas
significance: A long prose essay that criticizes the materialism and political corruption of postwar America while arguing that a literature equal to democracy does not yet exist. It is the document in which the poet states, in his own words, the political grounds of his poetics.

title: Specimen Days
significance: A prose collection that strings together his war-hospital records and his nature observations from his convalescence without regard to chronological order. Its composition, presenting fragmentary records as they are instead of a finished narrative, became a precedent for 20th-century nonfiction prose.

title: Poems by Emily Dickinson
significance: Her first poetry collection, assembled by acquaintances who selected from her manuscripts four years after her death, containing 115 poems. The editors revised her dashes and unconventional grammar to fit the norms of the day, but the first printing sold out quickly, and it was the book that first made her name known.

title: Poems by Emily Dickinson: Second Series
significance: A second gathering that followed the year after the first edition's success. As unpublished manuscripts kept being discovered, an unusual publishing situation arose in which one poet's collected poems continued to appear like a serial publication.

title: Letters of Emily Dickinson
significance: A posthumous collection of letters written in a style indistinguishable from her poetry. This book first revealed that her prose used the same compression and dashes as her poems.

title: Poems by Emily Dickinson: Third Series
significance: The last selection to appear under the early editorial policy. A definitive edition preserving the dashes and line breaks of her handwritten manuscripts had to wait for the scholarly editions of the mid-20th century.

title: The Birth of Tragedy
significance: His first book, explaining Greek tragedy as a tension between Apollonian form and Dionysian intoxication. Its departure from the procedures of classical philology got it rejected by the academic establishment, but it became the starting point for 20th-century theories of art that place art as a mode of knowledge.

title: The Gay Science
significance: A book that mixes and arranges aphorisms, poems, and maxims, in which the declaration of the death of God and the thought experiment of eternal recurrence are first presented. It is a case of redesigning the form of the philosophy book as a collection of fragments.

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
significance: An epic prose work borrowing the style of scripture, it appeared in four parts from 1883 to 1885, the last of which was printed in a small run at his own expense. Because it recasts argument into character and fable, it became a work of philosophy that reads as literature.

title: Beyond Good and Evil
significance: In 296 numbered aphorisms, it interrogates philosophers' prejudices and the grounds of morality. Because its narration displays a procedure of doubt rather than a conclusion, it is counted as the book in which his method is most compressed.

title: On the Genealogy of Morals
significance: In three consecutive essays, it traces how the concepts of good and evil, guilt, and asceticism were historically made. The genealogical method — the view that values are not natural facts but made things — is formulated here for the first time.
